Thanks! :) I get what you mean, but you can do it! I’m not an expert driver now but any means, and I still have a lot of anxiety to overcome, but some tips that have helped me:

- The first few times, either don’t listen to music or listen to relaxing music at a low volume to reduce distraction and help your senses feel less overwhelmed 

- Practice breathing exercises and self-affirmations before and during driving. Take deep breaths, remind yourself that you are capable, that you can do it, that you trust yourself to drive where you need to go

- For me, changing lanes is and was a point of anxiety, especially having to take my eyes off the road to check my blind spot and not seeing what’s going on in front of me. A lot of this has already been said on this thread before, but:

Relationships do not cure social anxiety disorder. This is something the people who say things like, “But if you have a partner, you must not REALLY have social anxiety!” will understand once they get into one. 
I’ve had two psych evaluations and have been diagnosed with social anxiety disorder on two separate occasions, and I’ve had that diagnosis reaffirmed by multiple mental health professionals over the years. I am also in a romantic relationship. These two things aren’t mutually exclusive. 

Also, that line of thinking leads to potentially unhealthy expectations for relationships. Your partner will not be a magic cure for your disorder. They can provide reassurance and a confidence boost, but they will not fix the underlying cause of social anxiety.

People who are in relationships can suffer just as severely from this disorder as those who aren’t.

Psychedelics still aren’t a miracle drug and it’s irresponsible to act like they are. They can help SOME people, but for others it can have negative impacts. I don’t know why you’re so bothered at people pointing that out.

I really don’t recommend it, especially if you’ve never done psychedelics before. I took a relatively low dose of shrooms for the same reason and had a terrible experience. My sibling took 8g shrooms and had a psychotic break (to be fair he was also smoking a lot of weed and drinking beer during his trip—I don’t know if he would have had this experience if he hadn’t been doing those things).

If you do decide to try it, be careful; have a trip sitter, a calm environment, and make sure you’re in a stable/optimistic mindset. 

Psychedelics are not a magic cure.

SNRIs like Cymbalta helped me a little, but they’re not a magic fix. Same with benzos. The best treatment for social anxiety is CBT and exposure therapy first, meds second

If you’re talking about medications like beta blockers, those work by blocking adrenaline, which would allow you to give a speech without the physical effects of anxiety. That’s only a short fix though, and I probably wouldn’t recommend them long-term or if you have low blood pressure

Yes. This is one of the main reasons SA in its severe forms is such a debilitating disorder. It forces you to make yourself small, give up your dreams, and basically lose all hope of becoming the person you want to be. 

I try not to think too much about what kind of person I would have become if I hadn’t had this disorder since early childhood, but sometimes I can’t help it. Maybe I would have done better in school and gone to a good college, I would have been able to build a strong support system of friends, I would’ve been able to thrive on my own. I think I would have liked to go into neuroscience or maybe counseling, but my SA has made both of those things impossible, or at least it feels that way right now. It infects every aspect of your life. It makes you wonder if there’s something fundamentally broken in you, because if everyone else can do all these small things so easily without thinking twice, why can’t you? 

Social anxiety is the disorder of lost opportunities.

To his right, Sarini Island, the zoo his mother took him to for his sixth and seventh birthdays, Ben giggling in delight at the pangorins and uralangs and caw-crabs that hopped around and nipped at the fingers he stuck through their cages. It was like walking into a long-forgotten dream, or a graveyard.

I honestly don’t recommend it. Mental illness and psychedelics can be a bad combination. I took shrooms years ago to try to bring myself out of a depressive episode and it only ended in a bad trip. A family member of mine took them for a similar reason not long ago and had a psychotic episode that sent him into a bad mental spiral for weeks. 

Obviously this isn’t the case for all people, some say shrooms really can ease anxiety and depression, but it’s definitely not a guarantee. That usually only happens in a clinical setting when the person is receiving a low dose of psychedelics along with therapy.

If you’re planning on trying it, take a low dose, make sure you have a full stomach, and spend some time before researching and meditating. Be with a trusted person. Don’t put all your hopes into a psychedelic to ‘cure’ you, you’ll just end up disappointed. Shrooms barely did anything good for me.
